thesis: Multimodal foundation models choose the right name far more often than they can state it. We call this the seeing-without-naming gap.
why_naming: Naming the organism in an image is the entry point to many agricultural decisions, from pesticide selection to breed management.

Multimodal foundation models are increasingly used as generative assistants: a farmer photographs a plant or an insect and asks what it is, and the model must answer with a name. In such use no list of candidate names is supplied, so open-ended naming, not choosing among options, is the task that matches practice.

AgriTaxon therefore measures how much agricultural visual knowledge a model holds. Naming is the first threshold for applying these models in agriculture, since advice on managing a crop, breed, pest, or weed depends on first knowing what it is.
abstract: Naming the organism in an image is the entry point to many agricultural decisions, from pesticide selection to breed management. Multimodal foundation models hold ever broader world knowledge, yet agriculture remains among their least evaluated domains. Its visual knowledge is fine-grained and long-tailed, with many regional species and breeds. We introduce AgriTaxon, a benchmark built from agricultural knowledge bases. Starting from the crops, breeds, pests, and weeds catalogued by FAO Ecocrop, FAO DAD-IS, and EPPO, it keeps 6,049 entities after filtering for image quality and entity validity. Each entity is linked through Wikidata, labeled at species level or finer, and evaluated in two settings: choosing its name among four options, and naming it without options. An LLM judge, validated against expert annotation, credits aliases. We comprehensively evaluate 17 proprietary and open-source models from eight providers. The best reach 85.8% multiple-choice accuracy but only 47.3% open-ended accuracy, and this seeing-without-naming gap remains after aliases are credited. The gap is harder to close for rare entities and field images. AgriTaxon-Hard isolates 510 entities that nearly all models fail. In AgriTaxon-Wild, one field image is about eight points less accurate for naming than the curated image, and only several images recover the loss. Naming accuracy rises with entity popularity and image resolution. A simple agentic loop with web retrieval already raises accuracy on AgriTaxon-Hard from 4.6% to 23.2%, making tool use a promising direction. Naming, which closed-set evaluation hides, thus remains the first threshold for applying foundation models in agriculture.
highlights: AgriTaxon: 6,049 knowledge-grounded entities across crops, livestock, pests, weeds
Seventeen multimodal models pick the right name far more often than they produce it
Best models: 85.8% multiple-choice accuracy vs. 47.3% open-ended naming accuracy
Popular entities are named by over six times as many models as rare ones
One field image lowers naming accuracy; web retrieval lifts Hard from 4.6% to 23.2%

main.name: AgriTaxon-Main
main.selection: Linked to FAO or EPPO; species level or finer

hard.name: AgriTaxon-Hard
hard.selection: At most 2 of 14 models correct in multiple choice

protocol.selection: Multiple-choice selection (MC): the model chooses the label among four options (A-D), the label and three distractors. The distractors are the three labels nearest to the answer by text embedding (Qwen3-Embedding). An answer is correct only when the returned option letter matches the label.
protocol.naming: Open-ended naming (OE): the model states the name of the entity without options.

metrics.MC accuracy: Share of items where the chosen option is the label.
metrics.OE-EM: Share of predictions that match the label exactly after normalization; a reproducible lower bound.
metrics.OE-Acc: Exact match, or a prediction the LLM judge accepts as an alias of the label (common name, synonym, spelling variant). The judge is an open-weight model (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) run with greedy decoding.

protocol.aggregation: Summary scores are unweighted means over the four tracks, so each track counts equally.

judge_validation: On a stratified sample of 579 predictions that fail exact match, weighted to all 72,997 such predictions of the 15 models evaluated when the judge was validated, the judge agrees with expert annotation on 97.8% (Cohen's kappa 0.84), against 92.8% for exact match. Correcting each model's OE-Acc for the judge's estimated errors changes it by -0.4 to +2.2 points, and the ranking is unchanged.

findings.title: Models select far more names than they can state
findings.text: Given four options, the best models reach 85.8% MC accuracy; asked for the name, the best model reaches 47.3% OE-Acc. For every model, OE-Acc is 36.8 to 60.2 points below MC accuracy. Crediting aliases adds only 3.7 to 14.5 points over exact match, so the gap does not come from unrecognized aliases.

findings.title: Open-source models trail by more in naming
findings.text: Among open-source models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches the highest MC accuracy (78.6%) and Kimi-K2.5 the highest OE-Acc (32.0%), 7.2 and 15.3 points below the best proprietary scores.

findings.title: Which track is hardest depends on the setting
findings.text: In multiple choice, Livestock is the easiest track for every model and Pest the hardest for 11 of 17. In naming, Weed or Crop has the highest OE-EM for 16 models and Pest the lowest for 12.

findings.title: Most naming errors confuse related taxa
findings.text: In a sample of 60 errors of Gemini 3 Pro, 70% name a related but wrong taxon of the same family, often the same genus.

findings.title: The gap is concentrated in the long tail
findings.text: Entities with at most 100 monthly Wikipedia views are named by 1.82 of 17 models on average, against 12.08 above 10,000 views, more than six times as many. 2,270 entities (38%) are in the least viewed bin, 61% of them pests, and no model names 54.1% of them.

findings.title: AgriTaxon-Wild: more field images, better naming
findings.text: On AgriTaxon-Wild, one field image is less informative than the Wiki image, but three or five overtake it. From one to five field images, OE-Acc rises by 20.8 points for doubao-seed-2-0-lite (40.3 to 61.1) and 13.6 for qwen3.5-35b-a3b.

findings.title: Tools recover hard entities
findings.text: On AgriTaxon-Hard, in a simple agentic loop, web retrieval raises GPT-5 Mini from 4.6% to 23.2% MC accuracy, and image cropping raises Claude Haiku 4.5 from 7.2% to 15.2%, making tool use a promising direction.

wild_results.caption: AgriTaxon-Wild results (%) on the 2,826 aligned entities, unweighted mean over the four tracks. Wiki image: the same entities with their single Wiki image; K: number of field images.

tool_results.caption: MC accuracy (%) on the 501 AgriTaxon-Hard entities covered by the tool runs.
tool_results.notes: Image cropping: the model can call a deterministic image_crop operator up to twice per item, each extracting a 448x448 region it specifies. Web retrieval: web_search and read_webpage, about 17 tool calls per item; no curated agricultural database is supplied.

popularity.caption: Mean number of the 17 models that select the correct name (MC) and that name the entity, aliases credited (OE-Acc), by monthly Wikipedia pageviews and by Wiki image resolution (megapixels), over all 6,049 entities.
popularity.resolution_note: Resolution is nearly unrelated to popularity (Spearman rho = 0.08). A sharper image helps naming, but much less than popularity.

errors.caption: The five types of naming errors in a sample of 60 errors of Gemini 3 Pro on AgriTaxon.

rows.label: Eastern tent caterpillar
rows.rationale: Same genus, Malacosoma. The model infers the genus from the communal silk tent but names the Eurasian lackey moth instead of the North American M. americanum.

rows.label: Gleditsia triacanthos
rows.rationale: Cross-family error: Fabaceae vs. Juglandaceae. Both are deciduous North American trees, but they are morphologically distinct.

rows.label: Cydia toreuta
rows.rationale: The model fails to produce any name. Cydia toreuta is an obscure tortricid moth.

rows.label: Licuala ramsayi
rows.rationale: The response is truncated or malformed, outputting the literal word "answer" instead of a species name.

rows.label: Swiss Warmblood
rows.rationale: The model identifies the animal as a horse but does not name the breed, producing a broader name where the breed is required.

construction: Wikidata links each entity to its FAO Ecocrop, FAO DAD-IS, or EPPO record and to its Wiki image (Wikimedia Commons).
EPPO entries are sorted into pests and weeds; pathogens, host plants and other entries are excluded.
Every label is at species level or finer (for livestock, usually a breed); genus- and family-level entities are removed, so a correct answer is always a name the image can support.
Wiki images with a shorter edge below 224 px are removed and those above the size limit are downscaled.
limitations: AgriTaxon focuses on naming an entity from its Wiki image, the step that begins any decision about a specific organism. Natural extensions: wider coverage, with more species and breeds (especially livestock breeds and pests) and images collected on farms; local and vernacular names in other languages, which the Wikidata links make possible; the decisions that depend on the name, such as host crops, quarantine status, or control options, using the linked FAO and EPPO records; and tools beyond the simple loop tested here, such as stronger agents, retrieval from the FAO and EPPO records, and tool use in open-ended naming.
